one_liner: Header-only SIMD substring search with a linear-time worst-case fallback; ~30x libc memmem on Apple M-series.
what_it_does: Finds the first occurrence of a byte pattern in a byte buffer, the job memmem/strstr/std::string::find already do. The API is not drop-in: simdsearch::find takes explicit length-delimited char pointers or a string_view and returns a {bool, index} pair or npos, as a free function with no searcher object to build. It handles arbitrary bytes (NUL, values above 0x7F, empty needles) and never reads outside the given ranges.
how_it_is_fast: Needle-Hammer picks 2-4 selective bytes from the needle as anchors and SIMD-filters 256 haystack positions per AVX-512 iteration (64 on NEON) against them, narrowing survivors byte by byte. A per-call work counter caps how much filtering it does; once the budget is spent on adversarial input it hands off to a Crochemore-Perrin two-way search, so every call stays O(n+m) instead of degrading like an unguarded anchor filter.
when_to_use: Substring/byte search over ordinary text or binary data on x86-64 with AVX-512F+BW, or any AArch64 core (NEON is architectural there)
Throughput-bound scanning (log grepping, large-buffer search) rather than a single short lookup, since the design targets memory-speed scanning
You can tolerate adversarial-input inputs falling back only to two-way's O(n+m), not needing sublinear worst-case behavior
You can vendor a header-only, dependency-free library and compile per target machine (a checked-in single header and single-header releases exist)
You need byte-exact, NUL-safe, non-UTF-8-aware search rather than a character-aware routine
when_not_to_use: Shipping one binary to x86-64 machines with unknown/mixed CPUs — there is no runtime dispatch; a CPU without AVX-512F+BW hits an illegal instruction
Targeting mainstream x86-64 client parts (most Intel client chips have AVX-512 fused off, pre-Zen4 AMD lacks it) or 32-bit/RISC-V/POWER, all unsupported
Building with MSVC — unsupported, since the headers use GCC/Clang builtins and attributes
Needing a licensed dependency for production use — the repo ships no LICENSE file
Wanting a published, apples-to-apples comparison against std::search or std::string::find — the benchmark driver includes both but no numbers for them are in the README

integration.dependencies: none for the library itself; the benchmark driver additionally fetches a 'counters' library and StringZilla via CPM (network access needed at configure time) and can optionally link Rust's memchr crate
integration.min_toolchain: C++17 for the library (GCC 14+ or a recent Clang, tested on GCC 14/15 and Apple clang 17); the benchmark driver needs C++23 for std::print; MSVC unsupported
integration.platforms: x86-64 requiring AVX-512F and AVX-512BW at compile time with no runtime dispatch, or AArch64 with NEON; other architectures fail to compile with #error
integration.thread_safety: Documented as reentrant and thread-safe: no allocation, no global or static state; needle preprocessing happens fresh inside every call with nothing to amortize across calls
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — matches memmem/std::string::find first-occurrence semantics, but the call shape differs: explicit length-delimited pointers or string_view in, {bool,index} pair or npos out, no iterators

gotchas: No runtime CPU dispatch: an AVX-512-compiled binary executes illegal instructions on hardware without AVX-512F+BW; the caller must detect the CPU and keep a fallback path itself
find_unguarded skips the work-counter guard entirely (a few percent faster on ordinary text) but reverts to O(n·m) worst case; documented as safe only on input the caller controls

Tuning constants (NH2_START_ANCHORS, NH2_BUDGET_DEN, etc.) were fitted on Emerald Rapids, Zen 5 and Apple M4 Max; the README says you shouldn't need to touch them but does not claim they are optimal on other hardware
No LICENSE file anywhere in the repo, so there is no stated legal basis for use, modification, or redistribution
pick_this_over_siblings_when: The catalogued siblings (sb_lower_bound, scandum/binary_search, SIMD Quad search, FastBinarySearch) all accelerate binary search over sorted arrays; simdsearch instead accelerates unsorted substring/byte search, i.e. memmem/strstr territory. Pick it when the task is finding a byte pattern inside a buffer, not locating a key in an already-sorted sequence.
verified_claims_summary: The README claims about 45 GB/s substring-search throughput on an unnamed Apple M-series core, roughly 30x the platform's libc memmem, measured on ordinary text at memory speed. The repo's own benchmark/README.md notes Apple's memmem 'uses a much simpler scan and lands well behind strstr,' so the 30x figure is against a weak platform baseline, and the top-level README tells readers to reproduce numbers on their own machine rather than publishing a results table for this specific claim.
status_note: Active: created 2026-07-28, last commit 2026-09-21, with one merged PR already fixing kernel correctness issues, but it is a brand-new, single-contributor project (9 stars, no LICENSE file), so treat it as reference material rather than something to depend on directly.
